question: A senior risk analyst at a SGD 60 billion Singapore pension fund is presenting the history of asset pricing theory to newly hired analysts. She wants one slide to capture what made the CAPM revolutionary when it was formulated in the 1960s. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: Before the CAPM, risk was usually measured by an asset’s covariance with the market; the CAPM replaced this with the asset’s own volatility, which is simpler to estimate.
options.B: The CAPM showed that an asset’s own volatility is irrelevant to investors in every model of risk, a conclusion that later factor research has fully confirmed.
options.C: The CAPM held that the risk of an asset is not how it behaves in isolation but how it moves in relation to other assets and the market, measured by its covariance with the market portfolio (its beta).
options.D: The CAPM held that the risk of an asset is how it covaries with whatever portfolio the individual investor already owns, so the relevant beta differs from one investor to the next.

solution:
Q1: A pension-fund analyst picks the statement that captures what made the CAPM revolutionary.

**Concept and theory**

Any pricing model must answer one question first: what is “risk”? Before the CAPM, the common answer was an asset’s own volatility, the spread of its returns looked at on their own. The CAPM (Treynor, Sharpe, Lintner and Mossin, building on Markowitz’s mean-variance diversification) was the first cogent theory to say that this is the wrong lens. An investor never holds an asset in isolation; she holds it inside a diversified portfolio, and in CAPM equilibrium that portfolio is the market. What matters is therefore how much the asset adds to the risk of the market portfolio, which is its co-movement with the market:

question: The chief risk officer of a BRL 25 billion Brazilian asset manager is reviewing a draft board memo that explains how the CAPM treats factor risk. options.A: The CAPM allows several systematic factors, with the market the most important, and an asset’s risk premium is the sum of its exposures to each factor times that factor’s premium.
options.B: Under the CAPM both an asset’s exposure to the market and its idiosyncratic risk earn risk premiums, but the premium on idiosyncratic risk is smaller because it can be partly diversified.
options.C: The single CAPM factor is the market return in excess of T-bills, and any asset whose total volatility equals the market’s volatility earns exactly the market risk premium.

solution:

**Concept and theory**

Factor theory says assets earn premiums because they are bundles of factor risks; it is the factor exposures, not the asset labels, that are rewarded. question:
A risk consultant is advising the investment committee of a GBP 4 billion UK university endowment on how the CAPM links risk premiums to bad times. She drafts the following statements.

I. In the CAPM, bad times are defined as periods of low (or negative) returns on the market portfolio.

II. An asset that tends to pay off when the market has losses has a low beta, and investors accept a low expected return to hold it.

III. High-beta assets must offer high expected returns because, with investors risk averse on average, the gains these assets deliver in good times do not cancel out their losses in bad times.

IV. In the CAPM, bad times are periods of high inflation or low economic growth, whichever the individual investor fears more.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I, II and III only
options.B: I and II only
options.C: I, III and IV only
options.D: II, III and IV only

solution:
Q5: An endowment’s consultant decides which statements correctly link CAPM risk premiums to bad times.

**Concept and theory**

Factor theory says every factor defines a set of bad times, and investors exposed to losses in those bad times are paid premiums in normal times. The CAPM has one factor, the market, so it has one definition of bad times: low (or negative) market returns. The logic, from GARP Lesson 6:

- An asset that loses when the market loses has a high beta. Investors are risk averse on average, so the gains it delivers in good times do not cancel out the pain of its losses in bad times. It is risky and must offer a high expected return to be held in equilibrium.

options.A: Investors care only about the mean and variance of portfolio returns, so they treat a loss and a gain of the same size symmetrically.
options.B: Investors hold only financial wealth, so labour income and liabilities play no role in their portfolio choice.
options.C: Individual investors are price takers, so no investor’s trades are large enough to move prices.
options.D: Taxes and transaction costs are permitted provided they are identical across all securities, because uniform frictions leave relative prices unchanged.

**Concept and theory**

Each CAPM assumption has a precise content, and exam traps usually corrupt one word of it.

- Mean-variance utility: investors care only about mean and variance, so risk is treated symmetrically; more realistic utility is asymmetric because investors are more distressed by losses than pleased by gains.
- Only financial wealth: investors’ unique income streams and liabilities are left out (in reality inflation, growth and labour income risk become factors).
- Price takers: individual investors cannot move prices.

Which of the following statements best describes the role of that assumption?

options.B: Because all investors share the same risk aversion, they all hold the same mix of the riskfree asset and the MVE portfolio, so in equilibrium the MVE portfolio becomes the market portfolio.

solution:
Q9: A French asset manager’s risk manager explains how homogeneous expectations turn the MVE portfolio into the market.

**Concept and theory**

Mean-variance investing on its own gives each investor a capital allocation line (CAL): a mix of the risk-free asset and the mean-variance efficient (MVE), maximum Sharpe ratio, tangency portfolio. The amount in each depends on the investor’s risk aversion. Nothing yet says the MVE portfolio is the market. The bridge has two steps.

1. **Homogeneous expectations.** Assume the set of means, volatilities and correlations is the same for all investors. Then all investors compute the same frontier and hold the same MVE portfolio, “just in different quantities depending on their own risk aversion”.

question: A member of the board risk committee of a USD 12 billion US charitable foundation is reviewing a consultant’s report that summarises the empirical standing of the CAPM. The member wants to check which summary is consistent with Ang’s assessment. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: Empirical studies broadly support the CAPM’s prediction that beta alone determines risk premiums, although its prediction that only one factor matters has been rejected.
options.B: Since both of its central predictions have been rejected, the CAPM has been abandoned by practitioners and its intuition about how risk is rewarded has been discarded.
options.C: The CAPM’s implication that every investor holds the market portfolio is strongly supported by data on investors’ actual holdings, even though beta pricing has failed.

solution:
Q10: A foundation board member checks a consultant’s summary of the CAPM’s empirical standing.

**Concept and theory**

Discussing the CAPM means knowing both what it predicts and how it has fared. Ang is blunt: the CAPM “is well known to be a spectacular failure”. It makes two central predictions:

1. asset risk premiums depend only on the asset’s beta, and
2. only one factor matters, the market portfolio.

“Both of these predictions have been demolished in thousands of empirical studies.” The implication that every investor holds the market portfolio is “outright rejected in data”. question:

Which statement is most accurate?

options.B: Diversifying across assets that are not perfectly correlated raises the Sharpe ratio, and market risk affects every investor except one who is infinitely risk averse and holds only risk-free assets.
options.C: Because diversification guarantees that losses on one asset are fully offset by gains on others, an investor who holds the market portfolio bears no risk that needs to be rewarded.

Pension fund analyst’s slide on why investors hold the market factor rather than individual assets.

**Concept and theory**

CAPM Lesson 1 is “don’t hold an individual asset, hold the factor.” The CAPM says there is exactly one factor, the market portfolio, in which every stock is held in proportion to its market capitalization (an index fund). Each individual stock has two pieces of risk:

| Piece of risk | CAPM treatment |
|---|---|
| Market (systematic) exposure | Pervasive, affects all assets; carries the risk premium (GARP’s “nutrient”) |
| Idiosyncratic (firm-specific) risk | Can be diversified away; earns no risk premium (“no nutritional value”) |

question:
A senior risk analyst at a German endowment is tagging historical quarters as “bad times” under a two-factor model in which factor 1 is the market portfolio and factor 2 is a value strategy (long value stocks, short growth stocks). Quarterly data are below; the last column was added by a colleague for a liquidity study.

| Quarter | Market return (%) | Value minus growth (%) | Avg. daily volume (EUR bn) |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | 6.2 | −4.1 | 11.8 |
| II | −8.7 | 2.9 | 19.4 |
| III | 3.5 | 1.6 | 9.7 |
| IV | −5.3 | −3.4 | 16.2 |

Which quarters are bad times under the two-factor model?

options.A: I, II and IV
options.B: II and IV only
options.C: IV only
options.D: I only

solution:
Tagging quarters as bad times under a market plus value two-factor model.

**Concept and theory**

In a multifactor model each factor defines its own bad times, and a period is a bad time if any factor is in its bad state. GARP’s investment-factor example uses exactly this model: “ $\text{f}_{1}$ could be the market portfolio and $\text{f}_{2}$ could be an investing strategy based on going long value stocks and short growth stocks . . . Bad times are characterized by low market returns, value stocks underperforming growth stocks, or both.” The CAPM, with the market only, would flag low market returns alone.

| Rule | CAPM | Two-factor model |
|---|---|---|
| Bad if market return low | Yes | Yes |
| Bad if value underperforms growth | No | Yes |
| Combination | Not applicable | “or both” |
